chunks: Stresses on a motor over its life. The question: What kind of stress may a motor experience in its lifetime?
Over its life, a motor faces four families of stress. Thermal stress is steady heat plus repeated heating and cooling.
Electrical stress is start-up surges, reversals, and voltage spikes. Mechanical stress is start-stop shocks, side loads, vibration, and overspeed.
Environmental stress is moisture, dust, and chemicals.
Many of these wear the motor by the count of events, not by hours of running, so you must start from how it will actually be used.
Bend a paper clip back and forth. One bend does nothing. Ten bends do nothing visible. But a few dozen and it snaps, even though no single bend was hard.
Motor stresses work like that: each start, each heat-up, each reversal does a tiny bit of damage that adds up.
All four stress families come from the same duty profile.
A design review should ask for the profile first, since a datasheet cannot know whether the motor will be started twice a day or twice a second.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates. It opposes the supply and grows with speed. Inrush current: the surge at start-up, before back-EMF builds up. It is V over R .
Plugging: reversing the supply on a spinning motor to brake it. Back-EMF adds to the supply.
Thermal cycling: repeated heating and cooling that fatigues solder, brush wires, and adhesives. Duty profile: the real pattern of loads, speeds, starts, and ambient conditions.
A 12 volts motor has a 1. 2 ohms coil (winding) and runs at 2 amps. At the instant of start, back-EMF is zero, so the current is 12 over 1. 2 equals 10 amps.
That is five times the running current and 25 times the heating. Now spin it to no-load speed, where back-EMF is 12 volts, and reverse the supply.
The current starts at (12 plus 12) over 1. 2 equals 20 amps, twice the stall current.
Separately, 20% overspeed raises the stress in the spinning rotor by 44%, because stress grows with speed squared.
That is the whole idea: list the stresses, put numbers on them, and design for the real duty profile.
"Four groups. Thermal: steady heat ages insulation and cycling fatigues joints. Electrical: inrush is V over R, so a 12 volts, 1.
2 ohm motor sees 10 amps at start, 25 times the heating of a 2 amps run; plugging can double stall current; plus inductive spikes and PWM edges stressing insulation and bearings.
Mechanical: start-stop shocks, side loads, vibration, overspeed. Environmental: moisture, dust, chemicals.
I'd soft-start, protect, derate, seal and qualify with cycling and life tests."
Quick check. A motor passes a constant-load life test but fails early in the field with frequent starts. What does this suggest?
